html:
The Finnish national epic, compiled by the doctor and folklorist Elias Lönnrot from folk songs he collected, mostly in Karelia. The first edition came out in 1835 and the longer, standard edition in 1849.

Lönnrot travelled on foot through remote villages, writing down songs that singers had passed on orally for centuries. He arranged them into one story, adding links of his own. It tells of the old wise singer Väinämöinen, the smith Ilmarinen who forges the magic Sampo, the reckless Lemminkäinen and the tragic Kullervo.

At the time Finland was a grand duchy of the Russian Empire, and its educated class spoke Swedish. The Kalevala showed that Finnish had a deep culture of its own. It fed the national awakening that led to Finnish becoming an official language and, in 1917, to independence. It inspired the music of Jean Sibelius and the paintings of Akseli Gallen Kallela, and Tolkien drew on it for his own myths. Finns mark Kalevala Day on 28 February.
